title: A Giant Arch in D.C.? How a Secret Club Pushed It Through
summary: Picture a huge golden arch, as tall as a 25-story building, right between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. That's what President Trump wants to build for America's 250th birthday. But here's the weird part: the design didn't come from a big, open competition like most famous D.C. memorials. Instead, it came from a small group of people close to Trump. Back in April 2025, a writer named Catesby Leigh suggested the arch on a website. He included two sketches—one by an architect named Nicolas Charbonneau and one by a group led by Rodney Mims Cook, Jr. Cook later became the head of the Commission of Fine Arts, the group that approves memorials. And guess what? Cook voted to approve the arch, even though it hadn't been reviewed by Congress or the public, which is usually required. Charbonneau works for a firm called Harrison Design. He posted his arch sketches on Instagram, and by October, Trump was showing donors models of the arch with a golden Lady Liberty statue on top. At the approval meeting in April 2026, Cook wore a hat that said "Make Design Great Again." Only one person on the seven-member commission was a trained architect. Historians are upset. For over 200 years, big memorials like the Washington Monument and Vietnam Veterans Memorial were chosen through open contests. Charles Birnbaum, a landscape architect, says this process "defied centuries of planning precedent and broken laws." The arch would sit on federal land managed by the National Park Service, which is now getting permits. Critics say a few people with a "narrow lens" are making a huge decision that should involve everyone.
why_it_matters: When a small group makes a big decision that changes a public space without asking others, it can feel unfair—just like if your school changed the playground rules without letting students have a say.

background_read: The National Mall in Washington, D.C., is a long park filled with famous monuments like the Lincoln Memorial (a marble building honoring President Abraham Lincoln) and the Washington Monument, and many were chosen through open design competitions.
The Commission of Fine Arts (a group of design experts created in 1910) normally reviews these projects after public input to make sure they fit into the city's historic landscape.
Arlington National Cemetery (where many American soldiers are buried) sits just across the river, so the arch would stand between two very special places.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Trump, Catesby Leigh, Nicolas Charbonneau, Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., the Commission of Fine Arts, National Park Service
WHAT: A giant golden arch proposed for America's 250th birthday was approved by a small group without the usual public review or Congress approval
WHERE: Washington, D.C., between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery on federal land
WHY: Critics say the secret decision-making ignored centuries of tradition, excluded the public, and broke laws meant to ensure fairness

perspectives.description: Supporters might say President Trump wants a grand symbol to celebrate the nation's history, and it could attract tourists and inspire pride.
Critics argue that the design process was secretive and unfair, bypassing the centuries-old tradition of open competitions that ensure everyone's voice can be heard.
Some point out that even great memorials can come from private ideas, but the lack of public review raises questions about fairness and the law.
